Now, let's move on to the proof that a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable.

A step function f is a function that can be written as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals. That is, f(x) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} c_i \* I_{[a_i, b_i]}(x), where I_{[a_i, b_i]}(x) is the indicator function of the interval [a_i, b_i], and c_i are constants.

To prove that f is Riemann Integrable, we need to show that the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same value as the partition of the interval [a, b] is refined.

Let P be a partition of [a, b] into n subintervals [x_{i-1}, x_i]. Let f_P be the step function obtained by evaluating f at the points x_i.

The upper Riemann sum U(f_P, P) is defined as:

U(f_P, P) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} M_i \* (x_i - x_{i-1})

where M_i = sup_{x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]} f(x).

Similarly, the lower Riemann sum L(f_P, P) is defined as:

L(f_P, P) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} m_i \* (x_i - x_{i-1})

where m_i = inf_{x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]} f(x).

Since f is a step function, we have that M_i = f(x_i) and m_i = f(x_i) for all i.

Now, let's show that U(f_P, P) and L(f_P, P) converge to the same value as the partition P is refined.

Let P_n be a refinement of P, obtained by adding more subintervals to P. Let f_{P_n} be the step function obtained by evaluating f at the points x_i.

We have that:

U(f_{P_n}, P_n) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} M_i \* (x_i - x_{i-1})
= ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i) \* (x_i - x_{i-1})
= ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i) \* (b_i - a_i)

Similarly,

L(f_{P_n}, P_n) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} m_i \* (x_i - x_{i-1})
= ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i) \* (x_i - x_{i-1})
= ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i) \* (b_i - a_i)

Since f is a step function, we have that f(x_i) is constant on each subinterval [x_{i-1}, x_i]. Therefore, the sum ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i) \* (b_i - a_i) is equal to the integral of f over the interval [a, b].

This shows that U(f_{P_n}, P_n) and L(f_{P_n}, P_n) converge to the same value as the partition P_n is refined.

Therefore, we have shown that the step function f is Riemann Integrable.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function f is defined on a closed interval [a, b]. If f is defined on an open interval (a, b), the proof is similar, but with some modifications to handle the endpoints.
